newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Britain's Iraqi exiles gloomy at Saddam's revival.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Britain's Iraqi exiles gloomy at Saddam's revival.

text.p: Six months after fleeing Iraq, Hassan dreams from exile about a day when President Saddam Hussein is toppled and his family can go home to a life free from fear.
"We want an end to him, so that we can see our homes again," said the 35-year-old former businessman, killing time over coffee with fellow exiles at a north London community centre.

Political refugees in Britain's large Iraqi community, the main centre outside the Middle East for rallying opposition to Saddam's quarter century-old rule, say exile is tolerable only as long as they can cling to a belief that they will one day go home.

But with Saddam still in power six years after his Gulf War defeat, the dissidents are watching in dismay as the defiant leader chips away at international sanctions and rebuilds oil and diplomatic connections.

Saddam's success in resuming limited oil exports, courting old friends like Russia and France and restoring his influence in Iraqi Kurdistan has dented the hopes of thousands of exiles desperate to abandon a life of loneliness and unemployment and rebuild a post-Saddam Iraq.
The gloomy prospect for the dissidents is more years of a safe but humiliating life of handouts on the margins of an alien society.

"Saddam is more in control than at any time since 1991. In my home city the people suffer increasingly from sectarian discrimination and a heavy security force presence," said Hassan, from the Shi'ite Moslem holy city of Najaf 180 km (110 miles) south of Baghdad.
"People inside Iraq know that there are common interests between the outside world and Saddam Hussein -- and interests are the bases of international relations."

Hassan's hopes soared in December when would-be assassins wounded Saddam's son and heir apparent Uday. But dissidents are divided about the accuracy of subsequent reports of turmoil inside Saddam's family.
"The army can topple Sassam with outside help. But Saddam's inner circle will never do it, because their fate depends on his," said Hassan.
Hassan's world collapsed last summer when he learnt Iraq's security services planned to arrest him on suspicion of opposition activities.
He immediately took his family and fled through neighbouring countries, joining other exiles in the West.
IRAQI COMMUNITY GROWING DURING SADDAM'S RULE

The Iraqi community, estimated at anywhere between 30,000 to 90,000, the second largest Arab group in Britain after Egyptians, has grown steadily during Saddam's rule. But many of the political refugees are ill-prepared to rebuild their lives, having fled Iraq to escape terror rather than to pursue economic opportunities abroad.

Hassan's family rely on local authorities for accommodation in small flats and on welfare payments for food. His belief that his exile is only temporary saps his desire to learn English and other job skills.

The political migrants, many of them lawyers, poets, writers, artists and journalists, have skills rooted in Arab culture that are of little use in Britain's economy. They say they face discrimination from potential British employers who fear they could be terrorists or criminals.
"People spend a lot of time thinking about relatives (in Iraq) and how to get them out of the country," said London University anthropologist Madawi al-Rashid,

"If there was stability after Saddam goes, you would get a lot of the most educated exiles going back to Iraq," said Yusuf al-Khoei, who runs a religious foundation and school for expatriate Iraqi families.
"You see people with doctorates driving minicabs," Khoei said. "For these people it is absolute hell to be here, whereas in a new Iraq they would have prominent positions."

"They just haven't tuned into life here in Britain. They develop all kinds of psychological problems," said Khoei, grandson of Shia Islam's top religious scholar, the late Grand Ayatollah Abolqassem al-Khoei.
IRAQIS KEEN TO GO HOME
Even some better-off migrants are keen to go home.

"I lead a very good life here, but we don't belong here," said Mowaffak al-Rubaie, a leading dissident and London neurologist who escaped to Britain in the 1970s. He has built a comfortable life but would not hesitate to return if Saddam were ousted.
"We like the British people. We like the freedom here. But we are not taking part in the life and decision-making of the country."

Migrants accuse the big powers of being content to let Saddam rule provided he gives business to international oil and commercial interests and desists from foreign adventures like his 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

But the Iraqi opposition is also weak and fractious. The most dissident groups can agree on is that Saddam should go. And even among Iraqis in Britain, there is a small but vocal pocket of Saddam supporters.

"Everyone feels betrayed," said Hamid al-Bayati of the opposition Supreme Council for the Islamic Revolution in Iraq. "The Iraqi people feel they were let down by the West. If you don't give someone help, you cannot expect concessions from them in the future.
"The interest of the West should be with the Iraqi people. The Iraqi people are going to be there forever. Saddam Hussein isn't."
